title: HTTP Requests and Responses
about: What your browser asks a website for, and what comes back.

cards.prompt:
Websites never push pages at you. Your [[browser]] has to **ask** for every file a page needs, one request per file.

A page is made of its text (one file) and 3 photos. Your browser has none of them saved yet. How many files does it ask for?
cards.explanation: One request for the text file, plus one for each photo: 1 + 3 = **4**. In fact the browser asks for the text first, reads it, and only then finds out it needs 3 photos. Big websites can need over a hundred requests for a single page.
cards.hint: Count every file the page is made of. Don't forget the text itself is a file too.
cards.nudge: The photos aren't the only files. The browser has to fetch the page's text as well, before it even knows about the photos.

cards.title: Ask and answer
cards.body:
That asking follows a [[protocol]] called **HTTP**. Your [[browser]] sends a **request**, like `GET /news`: a **method** (what to do) and a **path** (which page).

The [[server]] sends back a **response**: a **status code** saying how it went, then the **body**, the content itself. Web pages are written in **HTML**, the code that describes a page.

cards.prompt: Match each part of an [[HTTP]] conversation to its job.

pairs.right: What you want the server to do
Which page or file you want
The content itself, like the page's HTML

cards.explanation: The **method** is the action and the **path** is which item: those two travel in the request. The **status code** and the **body** come back in the response: first how it went, then the content.
cards.hint: Think of ordering at a café: what you want done, which item, whether they could do it, and what you actually get handed.
cards.nudge: Two of these go out in the request and two come back in the response. The status code is the short "how did it go" part.

cards.prompt: The two methods you'll meet most: **GET** means "please give me this", and **POST** means "please take this data". Which does your [[browser]] use for each?
cards.explanation: Watching, viewing and opening are all **fetching**, so they're **GET**. Commenting, logging in and uploading all **send your data** to the server, so they're **POST**. Most of your browsing is GETs; a POST happens whenever you press something like Send, Log in or Upload.
cards.hint: For each one, ask: is data coming **to** me, or am I sending something of mine **to** the server?
cards.nudge: Logging in may feel like "getting into" a site, but your password travels to the server. Which method carries data that way?

cards.prompt:
Every response starts with a three-digit **status code**, and its **first digit** says how it went:

- **2**: all fine, here it is
- **4**: a problem with the request, like asking for a page that isn't there
- **5**: a problem on the server

Sort these responses.
cards.explanation: Codes starting with **2** worked. **4** means the request was the problem: 404, the server looked everywhere and found nothing; 403, that page isn't yours to see. **5** means the server tripped over its own feet: 500 is an error inside it, and 503 means it's too busy or down for now.
cards.hint: Ignore the words for a moment and read only the first digit of each code.
cards.nudge: Some of the words sound alarming, but only the first digit decides. A 4 points at the request; a 5 points at the server.

cards.prompt:
`curl -I` (a capital **I**) asks a server for just the top of a response: the status code and some labelled lines called **headers**. A code starting with **3** means "this has moved", and a `Location` line gives the new address.

Run `curl -I http://example.com/old-news`. Where has that page moved to?
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Get the response headers for the home page
commands.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 1256
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 10:20:15 GMT
Server: nginx

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: http://example.com/news
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 169
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 10:20:21 GMT
Server: nginx

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 153
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 10:20:27 GMT
Server: nginx

cards.explanation: `/old-news` answered **301 Moved Permanently**, and its `Location` line gives the new address: `http://example.com/news`. A [[browser]] follows that by itself, so you'd just land on the new page. (The home page gave **200 OK**, and `/missing` gave **404 Not Found**, if you tried them.)
cards.hint: Run the command on `/old-news`, then look for the line that starts with `Location`.
cards.nudge: The first line only says the page moved. The new address is on a line of its own further down.

cards.prompt: A page shows **500 Internal Server Error**. What does that tell you about your own connection?

options.text: It works: a response arrived, so the fault is on the server
It's broken: your Wi-Fi probably dropped out mid-request
options.nudge: If your Wi-Fi were down, no response would arrive at all. Here a status code came back. What does that prove?

options.text: It works, but you probably typed the page's address wrong
options.nudge: A wrong address is a problem with the request. Which first digit did that kind of problem have?

options.text: Nothing: a 500 could mean your connection is working or broken
options.nudge: If your connection were broken, could any status code reach you at all? Think about how this one got to you.

cards.explanation: A **5** means the **server** had a problem. And the fact that any response arrived at all proves your connection, the address lookup and the route to the server all worked. A typo in the path would give a **4** code, like 404, instead.
cards.hint: Two clues: the first digit of the code, and the fact that a response arrived at all.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **HTTP**: the [[browser]] requests, the [[server]] responds.
- **GET** fetches things; **POST** sends your data to the server.
- Status codes: **2** fine, **3** moved, **4** request problem, **5** server problem.

Next: keeping all of this private with [[HTTPS]].
